title: Classes and Objects
relevance: Classes and objects are the core OOP construct in C++; interviews probe access control, stack vs heap allocation, object layout/size, and forward declarations.

phases.goal: Establish what a class and object are, what they contain, and default access plus definition syntax.

must_hit.point: A class is a user-defined type that acts as a blueprint; an object is a concrete instance built from that blueprint.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate separates blueprint (class) from instance (object) without conflating the two.

must_hit.point: A class lists data members (state) and member functions (behaviours); by default everything inside a class is private, so public must be specified for outside access.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions both data members and member functions, and that class members are private unless marked public.

must_hit.point: A class definition must end with a semicolon.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the trailing semicolon is required after the closing brace of the class.

probes: What is the difference between a class and an object in C++, and what is the default access for class members?

hints.1: Think blueprint versus instance, and what the language hides by default.
hints.2: List data members vs member functions, then say whether class members are public or private without an access specifier.
hints.3: Class = blueprint; object = instance; members default to private; the class definition ends with a semicolon.

phases.goal: Explain how objects are created and accessed, how member functions are defined, how size works, and what forward declarations allow.

must_hit.point: A stack object is declared like a local variable and members are accessed with the dot operator; each object holds its own independent copy of the data members.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives Account acc1; style construction and uses . for members; notes separate state per object.

must_hit.point: Heap allocation uses new, which returns a pointer; members are accessed with the arrow operator (->), equivalent to dereferencing then using dot; delete is required to avoid leaks.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows new Account(), pAcc->member, (*pAcc).member equivalence, and delete pAcc.

must_hit.point: A member function may be declared inside the class and defined outside using ClassName:: and the scope resolution operator.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Writes something like int Rectangle::area() { ... } after a prototype inside the class.

must_hit.point: Object size is determined by non-static data members (plus possible padding); member-function code is stored once and does not increase object size; an empty class has size 1 byte so each object has a unique address.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says sizeof reflects data members not methods; cites empty class size of 1 byte; may mention Point with two ints giving sizeof 8.

must_hit.point: A forward declaration introduces a class name without its layout; you may use pointers or references to the incomplete type, but not an object by value until the full definition exists.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Employee* is OK after class Employee; Employee emp; is not until the class is fully defined.

probes: How do you create an object on the stack versus the heap in C++, and how does that change member access? What determines sizeof an object?

hints.1: Contrast Account acc; with Account* p = new Account(); and what operator each uses.
hints.2: Cover ., -> (as (*p).), delete, out-of-line ClassName::, size from data members only, and forward-declared pointers vs by-value.
hints.3: Stack + . ; heap new + -> + delete; out-of-line uses :: ; size from non-static data (+ padding), functions shared, empty class 1 byte; forward decl allows pointers/references only.

phases.goal: Contrast where objects live and where member functions are defined, and when each choice is appropriate.

must_hit.point: Stack allocation creates the object directly as a local without new; heap allocation uses new and a pointer, requiring manual delete, and is the pattern closer to how languages like Python always place objects on the heap via references.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Compares Account acc1; (no new) with new Account() and notes Python-style heap/reference instantiation as a contrast.

must_hit.point: Defining a member function fully inside the class versus declaring it inside and defining it outside with :: trades inline convenience against keeping the class definition clean.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says out-of-line definitions keep the class body as prototypes only when you want a cleaner class definition.

probes: When would you allocate an object on the stack versus the heap, and why define a member function out-of-line?

hints.1: One path needs new/delete and a pointer; the other does not.
hints.2: Tie stack/dot vs heap/arrow/delete, then mention cleaning up the class body with ClassName::.
hints.3: Prefer stack for simple locals; heap when you need dynamic lifetime via pointer—and out-of-line :: when you want a slim class declaration.

phases.goal: Apply class/object rules to interview-style questions on layout, independence of instances, and incomplete types.

must_hit.point: For a class like Point with public int x and int y, sizeof(Point) reflects those data members (example output 8); move does not add to the object size because member functions are not duplicated per object.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Predicts sizeof from the two ints (8 in the example) and explicitly excludes the move function from the size.

must_hit.point: Two stack objects of the same class (e.g. acc1 and acc2) can hold different balances because each has its own data members; a Department can hold Employee* manager after only a forward declaration of Employee.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows independent state across instances and a pointer/reference to a forward-declared type in another class.

probes: What is the size of an object in C++? Can two Account objects have different balances, and can you store an Employee by value inside Department if Employee is only forward-declared?

hints.1: Ask what the compiler allocates per object versus once for the whole program.
hints.2: Sum non-static data members; functions are shared; incomplete types only work as pointers or references.
hints.3: Size = data members (+ padding), not methods; empty class 1 byte; instances have separate state; Employee emp; needs the full class, Employee* does not.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Stack: declare Account acc1; access with . ; no new. Heap: Account* pAcc = new Account(); access with -> (same as (*pAcc).); must delete to avoid leaks. C++ stack objects differ from Python, where objects are heap-allocated and held by references.

tradeoffs.topic: Inline member function vs out-of-line definition
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Define fully inside the class for locality, or declare inside and define outside with ClassName:: to keep the class definition clean while still operating on that object's data members.

gotchas.trap: Forgetting the semicolon after a class definition
gotchas.correction: The class definition must end with a semicolon; the compiler often reports the error on the next line or even in a different file.

gotchas.trap: Assuming C++ object creation works like Python Account() on the heap
gotchas.correction: In C++, Account acc1; instantiates directly on the stack without new; Python always instantiates on the heap via references.

gotchas.trap: Thinking member functions increase sizeof the object
gotchas.correction: Size comes from non-static data members (plus padding); member-function code is stored once in the text segment and does not enlarge each object; empty class size is 1 byte, not 0.

gotchas.trap: Using a forward-declared class by value
gotchas.correction: After class Employee; you may declare pointers or references (e.g. Employee* manager) but not Employee emp; until the full definition is available.

gotchas.trap: Forgetting delete on a new-allocated object
gotchas.correction: Heap objects created with new must be destroyed with delete to prevent memory leaks.
